 I made the change to wireless charging years ago, and thanks to the best wireless chargers I've been testing, I've never looked back. The convenience of having my phone (and sometimes my smartwatch and wireless earbuds too) powering up on my nightstand or desk without a cable in sight hasn't got old, and the variety of single and multi-device chargers is astounding.
 The majority of new smartphones work with Qi wireless charging, an open standard used by all sorts of chargers. But iPhones have their own MagSafe standard (or MagSafe 2 in the case of the iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 series) which has become a focal point for the best chargers on this list due to the popularity of Apple-made phones. But with the introduction of Qi2 , based on MagSafe, Android phones are becoming capable of using these chargers as well, either natively with the Google Pixel 10 series or with the installation of a magnet ring or specially-designed case.
 Because of the number of companies out there wanting to sell you a wireless charger, it can be hard figuring out what's good. For my money, the Belkin Boost Charge Pro 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Pad remains the best option for powering up your key wirelessly-charging gear, while Otterbox's Wireless Charging Pad is my pick for those wanting a basic, brand-agnostic charging experience for any device you like.

It's great for using StandBy mode, but if you like your iPhone vertical while charging, this charger's short height doesn't allow taller iPhone models to stand at a good angle.  How to choose the best wireless charger for you 
 To make sure you get the best wireless charger for your needs, you'll need to check what kind of wireless charging your phone supports. Most new wirelessly-chargeable phones are Qi-compatible, which lets them work with a wide range of products at either 7.5W or 10W of power. iPhones since the iPhone 12, as you might expect, have their own MagSafe standard that offers 15W of power when used with compatible accessories, or 25W in the case of an iPhone 16 and 2nd-gen MagSafe. Other companies like Samsung and OnePlus have their own wireless fast charging tech too, but you're less likely to find support for those in third-party products.
 There's also Qi2 to contend with now. This newer standard combines MagSafe and Qi technologies together, allowing for faster charging with magnetic fastening as an option. No phones other than iPhones support this by default yet, but we expect other companies to start adopting it on their devices soon.
 You'll also want to pay attention to whether a charger and charging cable are included in the box. If there is one included, look for a charger that supports Qualcomm's Quick Charge 2.0 or 3.0 technology, as these will ensure you get the maximum available speeds.
 If you want to be able to charge multiple devices at once, there are some 2-in-1 or 3-in-1 chargers available that can juice your phone, earbuds and smartwatch all at once, but you're going to pay more for these accessories.

 For price, it's obvious why the Otterbox Wireless Charging Pad is our top pick. In terms of features, it'll depend on your needs as to which is best. The Anker MagGo Wireless Charging Station is the best if you need something compact that'll still power up everything in your pockets and on your wrist. The Zens Quattro Charger Pro can't be beaten when it comes to charging multiple phones at full speed, with the Belkin boost Charge Pro still doing the best job at being portable but premium-feeling, and offering maximum speeds for an iPhone, Apple Watch and another smaller device.
 All these devices charge up to 15W in the case of a MagSafe-enabled iPhone. If you're not using a Qi2 charger though, non-iPhones will charge slower, so bear this in particular in mind when picking one.
 How we test wireless chargers 
 To put wireless chargers through their paces, we take them home and live with them for at least one week, charging all supported devices on them overnight as a test of regular charging, and a timed test during the day to see how quickly the charger can fill up an iPhone.
 All chargers are tested with their included cable and charger, or with a standard 30W charger and USB-C cable if required. We also assess the practicality, design, material quality and the usefulness of any special features during the testing period.
 FAQ 
 Which company's wireless charger is best?
 It's hard to pick one company as the ultimate in wireless charging, but of the brands represented on this list, we recommend Belkin, Otterbox and Nomad as our favorite wireless charger makers. But there are plenty of good ones out there!
 Which 3-in-1 wireless charger is best?
 The top 3-in-1 wireless charger on our list is the Belkin Boost Charge Pro 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Pad with MagSafe. In fact, we like it so much it's our overall top pick! It may not be the top choice if you aren't an iPhone user though, since it does utilize Apple's proprietary MagSafe connection.
 What is the fastest wireless charger?
 This is going to depend on what device you're using. If it's an iPhone 12 or newer for example, then it'll be any device that uses MagSafe and provides 15W of charging. Other phone makers have their own standards, and often the only compatible chargers are the ones they sell themselves.
 In terms of generic chargers, the fastest speed you'll get is the Qi standard of 7.5W. This isn't particularly speedy, but it'll work with any wirelessly chargeable smartphone, or other devices like wireless earbuds at slower speeds.
 Is 10W or 15W better for wireless charging?
 When it comes to smartphone charging, the general rule is the more watts, the faster your phone charges. Therefore 15W (the highest available form of the near-universal Qi charging standard) will power up your phone quicker.
However, your phone may not support 15W wireless charging, meaning you're better off with 10W, which your device may well still support. It's good to check your phone's specs before committing to one charger or another so you're getting the best possible speeds.

 Wireless charging has been around for more than a decade, but lots of people are still plugging in the old-fashioned way. But trust me: Once you free yourself from fishing for and fumbling with cables in the dark, you'll never want to go back. Dropping your phone on a pad or stand at the end of the day and waking up to a fully charged battery in the morning is easy and convenient. Yes, it’s slower than wired charging—but at night that hardly matters anyways.
 After testing more than 100 wireless chargers over the past decade, sorting the good from the bad ( there are certainly bad ones ), I have identified the best wireless chargers. You will find many pads and stands in different styles, shapes, and build materials with spots for other devices, alongside your phone.
 Check out our other buying guides , including the Best Android Phones , Best iPhones , Best 3-in-1 Apple Wireless Chargers , Best MagSafe and Qi2 Chargers , and Best MagSafe Power Banks .

It’s a weighty mix of metal and glass in black or white, with padding in all the right places. You get a nice braided cable in the box (USB-C to USB-C), but you will need a 40-watt charger ($25) , which is a bit cheeky at this price.

 Kew Labs’ UTS-2 is unlike any other wireless charger in this guide—it disappears completely. Designed to be mounted below nonmetallic surfaces—a nightstand, countertop, or desk—it sends power through the tabletop and to your smartphone or wireless charging-capable device. That way, you get a true wireless experience, at least visually. The recommended thickness for the surface you plan to install it under is between 8 and 12 millimeters.
 I tested the original UTS-1 , but the newer model is far less bulky, easier to install, and performs better. There's an adhesive back on the charger that stuck to my wood nightstand quickly, though you can screw it into place if you'd like. It comes with an alignment tool that lights up LEDs when you're perfectly over the charger—you can then attach one of the many included stickers to indicate the charging spot. It took me less than two minutes. Charging won't be fast—iPhones will top out at 7.5 watts, Samsung phones will handle 10 watts, and everything else is 5 watts. (It took roughly four to five hours to bring an iPhone 16e from zero to 80 percent.) But it's perfect when you want to maximize your table space and don't need to recharge quickly. — Julian Chokkattu

 Other Wireless Chargers We Tested
 There are a lot of wireless chargers. Here are a few more we like, but for one reason or another don't warrant a place above.
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Krafted Couch Wireless Charger for $52 : I thought this wireless charger that’s designed to be draped over the arm of your couch was a great idea when I saw it, but the ridges failed to keep it in place on my velvety couch, so it kept slipping down the side. The silicone finish with the Krafted logo is also a bit ugly. It's just a silicone mat with a magnetic charger inside, though there is a fairly generous 6.6-foot (2-meter) cable, and it is Qi2 rated. If you’re always rooting around for a charger and one of the colors blends well with your furniture, it might be a good solution for you.
 Nimble Apollo Wireless Pad for $19 : The silicone surface of this wireless charger easily accumulates dust and lint, but that might not matter to you if you're shopping for the most eco-friendly charger. It's made of recycled silicone, the texture of which helps keep phones from sliding off the surface. The rest of it is made with post-consumer plastic and alloy, and even the packaging is plastic-free. Better yet, if you have an iPhone 12 or newer with MagSafe, the magnets inside the Apollo will keep your iPhone aligned perfectly for more efficient charging, even if they're not as strong as normal MagSafe wireless chargers.
 Einova Eggtronic Charging Stone for $70 : Made with 100 percent solid marble or stone—you can choose from a variety. Every single pick in this guide looks very much like a wireless charger, but I've had visiting friends ask if this one is a drink coaster. (I'm still figuring out whether that's a good or bad thing.) It has zero LEDs, perfect for bedrooms; just try to hide the cable to truly make it blend into your home. We recommend putting a case on your phone when using it with this charger, as there's a risk of scuffing up the back with these harder surfaces. — Julian Chokkattu 
 Baseus Nomos 5-in-1 Magnetic Charging Station for $88 : If you liked the PicoGo W2 above but need more gadget-charging power, this 5-in-1 could be worth a look. It also has a tilting pad and retractable USB-C cable, three USB-C ports, and one USB-A. It’s perfect for your desktop.
 Rapport London Formula Wireless Charging Tray for $475 : Yes, this is an obscene price for a Qi wireless charger. You can probably make a version for a fraction of the cost. But Rapport's build quality is quite nice, with a lacquered grey box and a soft-touch fabric to keep your watches and phone scratch-free. It reliably recharged several Android phones without making them too warm, all while offering storage for a few watches. It's attractive, but you have to have cash to burn at this price. — Julian Chokkattu 
 iOttie iOS Wireless Duo for $80 : This dual-charging system looks pretty—I like the fabric-wrapped stand—and you can charge another device on the rubberized charging pad next to it. The stand can be used in portrait or landscape, though in the latter orientation it'll block the pad. I use the pad to top up my wireless earbuds, but I wouldn't use this iOttie on a nightstand, because the LED on the front can be glaring. A cable and adapter are included, which makes it a good value. It can charge Pixel phones at up to 15 watts, iPhones at 7.5 watts, and other Android phones at 10 watts. — Julian Chokkattu 
 Journey Alti Play Performance Desk Mat for $120 : This is a desk mat that doubles as a wireless charging pad. On the left side is a plasticky rectangle with a Qi2 magnetic puck for your smartphone. Above it is a little area to charge wireless earbuds (5 watts). Naturally, there's RGB all over, and there are two buttons you can press to cycle through patterns and colors. It's a smart-looking system, though the quality of the actual mat leaves a bit to be desired. I didn't have issues gliding my mouse on it, and it stays put thanks to the rubber underside, but I just didn't like the look and feel of the Lycra surface. Journey has some other versions of this mat that use different materials , so take a look if you like the overall aesthetic. — Julian Chokkattu 
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Zens Liberty Wireless Charger for $150 : I tested the Glass Edition of this wireless charging pad, and it looks stunning with the 16 overlapping copper coils on display (the standard version has a woolen fabric top). It can charge two devices simultaneously at up to 15 watts apiece. As stylish as it is, the price is too high. Because you can see the coils, placement is never an issue, but it’s a bulky charger; the fan is audible at times, and while I had no problem charging my iPhone or AirPods, my Pixel 6 Pro got very warm on this pad.
 Courant Catch:2 Essentials for $75 : Wireless chargers should look nice. You shouldn't settle for anything less! This Courant dual charger oozes luxury with its Belgian linen-wrapped surface (especially in the camel color). I've used it by my front door to recharge my partner's and my wireless earbuds for two years. The rubber feet prevent it from shifting around, but even if there are five coils in this pad, you should try to be precise when you put your device down to charge and make sure the LED lights up to double-check. It comes with a color-matching USB-C cable. — Julian Chokkattu 
 Xiaomi Mi 80-W Wireless Charging Stand for $80 : By far the fastest wireless charger we have tested, this stand is only worth considering for Xiaomi phones (it seems to charge most other phones at 10 watts or below). I tested with the Xiaomi 13 Ultra , which tops out at 50 watts (some Xiaomi models can go higher). The unusual sail shape combines a white triangular section with a clear acrylic base that has a subtle groove to hold your phone in place and a gap underneath for the exhaust grill from the noisy fan. The USB-C port and LED indicator are on the back.
 Does My Phone Support Wireless Charging?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Not all phones support wireless charging, but most brands have models that do, so look up your phone model first. You'll usually see "Qi wireless charging" (the default standard) or simply "wireless charging" if it does on the product page or specs list.
 Phones that support the latest Qi2 standard bear the Qi2 logo and have a ring of magnets for easy alignment (just like Apple's MagSafe). Qi2 is backward compatible, so Qi phones can be charged on Qi2 chargers, though they may charge at a slower rate. Sadly, this does not always apply the other way round, as we discovered with the HMD Skyline (the first Qi2 Android phone), which cannot be charged with all Qi chargers.
 Some phones are also Qi2 Ready , like Samsung's Galaxy S25 series . This means they have the necessary arrangement inside to enable Qi2 functionality—faster charging, more efficient energy transfer—but they don't have built-in magnets. To enable the full Qi2 magnetic wireless charging capability, you need to pair the phone with a Qi2 Ready case with magnets inside. The latest update, Qi2 25W, allows for a faster maximum charging rate of 25 watts, up from 15 watts. Supported phones include the iPhone 17 range and Google's Pixel 10 Pro XL .
 Do Wireless Chargers Work With Phone Cases?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Yes, most wireless chargers can charge through cases, unless it's a particularly thick case. Check the product listing—there's usually a case thickness limit in millimeters. Phones can get hot when charging wirelessly, so don't worry if your phone is really warm when you pick it up. Most smartphones have limits to stop accepting a charge if they get too hot.
 If you have a MagSafe charger or a Qi2 charger with magnets, you can use a magnetic case even if your phone doesn't support those standards. You may not be able to take advantage of all the features, but it should deliver basic wireless charging that's more precise thanks to the magnets.
 Yes, Cords Will Charge Your Phone Faster
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Some manufacturers like Apple and OnePlus make wireless chargers that recharge their respective phones faster than others, but if you're looking for the speediest phone charger, you're better off sticking with a cord. Wireless charging is best for desks or nightstands when you're not really using your phone or in a rush to recharge it. Check out our Best USB-C Cables guide if you need one, though the cable that comes with your phone should be sufficient.
 What's a Fast Wireless Charging Speed?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Most MagSafe and Qi2 chargers can go up to 15 watts, and there are a handful of proprietary wireless chargers for specific phone models that can charge even faster. The latest Qi2 25W standard allows for charging up to 25 watts. It's worth noting that, even where phones support them, the maximum charging rates are only reached some of the time (the charging rate is automatically adjusted to preserve battery health). Many older iPhones are capped at 7.5 watts for wireless charging and many older Android phones are capped at 10 watts. We have included the maximum wireless charging rate in the specs table for each entry. Remember that the charger also requires the correct cable and power adapter to charge at its maximum rate.
 Is Wireless Charging Safe?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 There's no definitive evidence that it's harmful. You may worry the phone's battery might degrade faster with wireless charging, but manufacturers set safe limits for phone batteries, stipulating how much a battery can be charged and how far it can discharge. Regardless of the charging source you use, whether you plug into a wall adapter or use a wireless charging pad, these limits can’t be overridden. There’s no risk of overcharging your phone by leaving it on a wireless charger all night.
 How Do I Keep My Phone's Battery Healthy?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Try to keep your battery between 50 and 80 percent for optimum battery health . Keeping your phone fully charged or fully discharging the battery will degrade it slightly faster, and regularly swinging between full and empty will shorten its life. Battery technology has improved in recent years, and phone batteries are more reliable than ever. If you switch phones every two to three years or don’t mind paying a modest fee for a battery replacement on that timescale, it’s not worth worrying too much about how often or when you charge your phone.
 What Is the Downside of Wireless Charging?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 The main downside is that wireless charging is slower than wired charging. Wireless charging is less efficient, because some of the power is lost as heat. Original Qi chargers are only around 60 to 75 percent efficient. Qi2 chargers manage 75 to 80 percent efficiency, but wired charging is typically 85 to 95 percent efficient.
 How I Test Wireless Chargers
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 I test every wireless charger for at least a week, using it to charge both my Pixel 10 Pro XL and iPhone 16. I also test with an older iPhone 12 and Pixel 9. I live with most chargers on my nightstand or work desk. Where possible, I check the charging rate and note the time it takes to charge my phone. I assess the usability of the design and the strength of the magnets, test any additional charging ports or pads, and try out any special features.

 What is it? A premium 3-in-1 Qi2 wireless charging stand with active cooling and a built-in power display.
 Who is it best for? iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods owners who want a stylish desktop charger with fast wireless charging and detailed power information.
 Who should skip it? Light sleepers, frequent travelers and users who don’t need active cooling or a charging display.
 Ugreen’s MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Charging Stand 25W looks different to most wireless charging stands on the market. It’s not a classic charging tree design like the Anker Prime 3-in-1 MagGo Charging Station or Belkin BoostCharge Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand , nor a squat stand, flat pod, or cube.
 It closely resembles a modern-day reimagining of the old-style Shure Elvis microphone, with its large silver circular iPhone-charging module ringed with air vents on the sides and a large fan at the rear. It’s not shy of being a statement piece on your desk or nightstand, or frightened to show off its iPhone cooling tech. The iPhone charging module can tilt more than 90 degrees. The Watch module can lie flat or be raised for Nightstand Mode.
 How fast does the MagFlow Pro charge each device?
 iPhone: up to 25W (iPhone 16 and later); 15W (earlier iPhones)
 Apple Watch: 5W
 AirPods case: 5W
 Those specs mean it should fast-charge each device, although speeds will decrease when all three are used simultaneously—with a maximum output of 32.5W. It ships with its own 45W wall charger so is well covered by that. Although the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 doesn’t include a spare USB-C port itself—look to Mophie’s StealthCharge 4-in-1 Charging Stand for extra ports and cables—you could simply use the Ugreen wall charger for your MacBook, although not as speedily as the iPhone, Watch, or AirPods.
 If 25W charging can be sustained, an iPhone could reach 50% in around 30 minutes; 45 minutes at 15W.
 An Apple Watch, such as the Series 11, should charge from 0-50% in about 20 minutes.
 (We use the 0-50% measurement as batteries charge slower as they get fuller, so the first 50% of a charge is the best comparison when testing different units.)
 The fan at the back of the MagFlow Pro is the largest we’ve seen on any wireless charger. Simon Jary
 How does the MagFlow Pro stay cool?
 All that high-powered charging generates heat, especially for the iPhone that can reach 25W for iPhones 16 and later (15W for earlier iPhones).
 Most gadgets don’t like hot temperatures that can damage battery life and the iPhone has built-in safeguards that throttle the incoming power if it feels that it’s getting too warm. That means the 25W might be slowed to 15W or less, and even turned off until the phone cools down by itself.
 To reduce the threat of the iPhone dialling back the power and therefore the charging speed, Ugreen employs active cooling via the built-in fan. Ugreen calls the 15dB fan “ultra quiet” but you can hear it humming with a rushing wind sound. True, it’s nothing like setting off a hair dryer but it’s definitely audible.
 When you’re not in a rush to charge your iPhone, you can turn the cooling fan off with one of the easy-access side buttons (see below). This is certainly recommended if charging by your bedside at night, unless you’re a white-noise enthusiast. Charging overnight doesn’t require the highest speed anyway, so there’s no need for the fan as the iPhone will take in power as it feels fit while you sleep or while you’re working at your desk. But you can turn on the cooling blaster when you’re in a real hurry for power.
 Simon Jary
 What does the MagFlow’s display show?
 There’s a trend for chargers and charging stands to include a real-time display, and the MagFlow Pro’s display is on the front of the arm that suspends the iPhone charger.
 The TFT display shows charging wattage for each device, charging surface temperature, and cooling mode. Along the side of the arm are two buttons that you use to switch off the charger and its cooling mode, plus switch from one info-screen to another.
 I’m not sure many people other than gadget geeks and tech reviewers—quite the Venn diagram—are going to pay much attention to such in-depth charging data, but it’s handy if you’re a power data control freak.
 The MagFlow Pro’s Apple Watch charging module can lay flat when not in use, and be raised to work in Nightstand Mode. Simon Jary
 What’s it like to use every day?
 The MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is an attractive elevated charging stand for a desk or nightstand with tilting iPhone-charging pad, a non-slip AirPods case charging module at the front, and an adjustable Apple Watch charger sat at the back.
 It has a small footprint, with a 4.6-inch (117mm) base diameter. It weighs 19.1oz (541g). Charging stands require a decent heft to stay stable. If you want a more portable 3-in-1 travel charger, consider the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Folding Wireless Charging Station , Kuxiu X40 Turbo 25W Wireless Charging Stand , or ESR CryoBoost Foldable 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Station . Ugreen’s own $59 / £43 MagFlow 2-in-1 Foldable Magnetic Wireless Charger is also worth considering but lacks the Watch charger found on the other travel charger.
 iPhone shown in Decoded Silicone Case ; Apple Watch with UNIQ Revix IV PANTONE Edition Reversible Apple Watch Band . Simon Jary
 How much does the Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 cost?
 The Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is priced at $159.95 / £119.99 direct or on Amazon / Amazon UK .
 Check out our reviews of the best wireless charging stations for alternatives, although if you admire this form factor there’s nothing really to stop you ordering one right away.
 Should you buy the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand 25W?
 The Ugreen MagFlow Pro is an attractive, well-built charging stand that brings together fast Qi2 wireless charging, adjustable iPhone and Apple Watch charging pads, and a useful display showing real-time power consumption and temperature.
 Its standout feature is the built-in cooling fan, designed to help prevent heat from slowing iPhone charging. However, the fan is noticeably audible, which makes the MagFlow Pro better suited to a desk than a quiet bedside table.
 At $159.95/£119.99, it’s a premium option, and cheaper 3-in-1 chargers will meet the needs of users who simply want to charge their Apple devices overnight. But if you value its distinctive design, cooling system and detailed charging information, the MagFlow Pro has plenty to offer.

 Offering up to 25W power output in the right configuration, MagSafe charging is much faster than basic 7.5W magnetic wireless charging. The similar magentic Qi2 standard , supported by the iPhone 13-17 families (and unofficially the iPhone 12 but strangely not the latest 16e) offers similar 15W speed charging. Qi 2.2 , also known as Qi2 25W, meets MagSafe at 25W for iPhone 16/17 series.
 MagSafe or Qi2 certification
 Apple certifies MagSafe accessories to ensures that the output charging is 15W for most iPhones, and up to 25W for iPhone 16 and 17 (with Apple’s latest MagSafe charger or chargers certified for Qi2 25W). Non-certified magnetic but “MagSafe-compatible” chargers are usually just 7.5W with a ring of magnets to hold your phone in place. Certified MagSafe chargers also have a single-wire NFC antenna that allows the iPhone to identify the device and a built-in magnetometer to prevent compass interference while you are using your iPhone while it’s charging.
 In our tests, 15W MagSafe and Qi2 chargers are evenly matched for charging speeds. 7.5W MagSafe compatible chargers, as you might expect, take around twice as long—certainly in the early stages of charging. But don’t rule out 7.5W chargers as they are often high quality, nearly always noticeably cheaper and just take a while longer to fully charge an iPhone. The king of the hill is Apple’s new MagSafe charger and chargers based on the new Qi2 25W technology that are definitely faster at 25W, but only with iPhone 16 or later.
 Foundry
 Simple vs multi-device magnetic chargers
 The most basic form of MagSafe or magnetic charger is the simple pad that latches on to the compatible iPhone. Some pads feature a pop-out arm so the iPhone can be propped up while charging. There are also products that can simultaneously charge an iPhone plus other Apple devices, such as an Apple Watch or wireless AirPods charging case. Note that the AirPods case must be of the wireless variety, and the original AirPods case lacked this functionality. The base of a multi-charger could also be used to charge a second iPhone but mostly not magnetically and at 5W rather than 7.5W, 15W, or 25W. Also see our round up of the Best Apple Watch chargers and stands .
 Best simple MagSafe chargers
 A simple MagSafe charging pad is the cheapest route to wireless iPhone charging. If you are going to the bother of connecting this product to a wall charger, why not just use a Lightning (iPhone 14 or earlier) or USB-C (iPhone 15 and up) cable direct to the iPhone? You can fast-charge an iPhone to 50% battery in under 30 minutes using a cable and just over that using a 25W charger, while it takes around 50 minutes to wirelessly charge iPhone from 0 to 50% using even 15W MagSafe.
 That said, there are interesting options to choose from. After these we’ll look at more multi-functional MagSafe chargers.

With 25W wireless chargers you can simply place your iPhone on and know you should be able to charge it to 50% in around 30 minutes.

 MagSafe Monday: LISEN’s new desk charger brings 25-watt MagSafe charging with a built-in cooling fan
 Bradley C  | Feb 2 2026 - 1:56 pm PT 
 1 Comment 
 One of the most significant limitations of MagSafe charging is heat management. As induction coils transfer energy, they generate waste heat, which causes your iPhone to throttle its charging speeds if it gets too hot to protect the battery. You especially see this in the outdoors during the summer. LISEN is attempting to fix the normal thermal bottleneck with its new 3-in-1 MagSafe station . By adding an active cooling fan and the Qi2.2, LISEN claims it can sustain 25-watt charging speeds that really does wired charging. This is my current daily driver on my desk, and I really like it thus far.
 MagSafe Monday:  Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
 Active cooling and design
 The standout feature on LISEN’s new 3-in-1 desk charger is the active cooling system. We have seen fans in MagSafe car chargers before, but they are less common on desktop units because they aren’t exposed to outdoor weather. The goal is to keep the phone cool enough to maintain the peak 25-watt speed that Qi2.2 allows without throttling it to manage heat. The stand features a control to toggle between “Cool Mode,” where the fan is active, and “Sleep Mode,” where it runs silently. If you plan to place this on a nightstand, the ability to disable the fan is table stakes for me.
 The hardware itself feels really nice with a weighted chrome-plated base. It stays planted when you pull your phone off the MagSafe charger, which is a common annoyance with less expensive docks. The main puck supports both portrait and landscape orientations, making it a great option for StandBy mode. LISEN, thankfully, includes a 45-watt power adapter in the box, so you know you’re getting the best output.
 Qi2.2 charging speeds
 The headline feature of this unit is its 25-watt charging speed, which utilizes the Qi 2.2 standard. LISEN claims this can get an iPhone 17 Pro to 50% battery in about 22 minutes. That is a significant jump over the 15-watt cap you’ll see on a lot of MagSafe chargers. To reach those speeds, however, you need the fan running in “Cool Mode” to manage the heat generated by such high power throughput.
 If you are using this on a nightstand table, you will likely want to switch it to “Sleep Mode.” This turns off the fan for silent operation but effectively removes the active heat dissipation. For overnight charging, the speed reduction doesn’t really matter, but it is a distinction worth noting if you need a quick top-up while you sleep. The base also features a spot for your AirPods and Apple Watch, making it it is incredibly beneficial for all your gear. 
 Wrap up
 The bottom line here is speed. The ability to take an iPhone 17 Pro from dead to 50% in just 22 minutes is really handy and impressive. If you are the type of person who is constantly in and out of meetings around your office and you often find yourself with a low battery, this is the quickest way to top it off without hunting for a USB-C cable.

 Yes: A Qi2 25W (Qi2.2) certified charger, or Apple's current MagSafe Charger 
 Yes: iOS 26 or later on an iPhone 16, which third-party Qi2 25W makers list as a requirement

Choose Apple's MagSafe Charger if you want the reference puck and already own a 30W+ adapter, and the UGREEN MagFlow for the car.  Frequently asked questions
 What power adapter do I need for a 25W MagSafe charger? Apple says its MagSafe Charger needs a 30W or greater USB-C adapter rated at 15V/2.0A or higher to reach 25W. Apple's current MagSafe Charger is certified for Qi2 25W, and recent iPhones charge at up to 25W on either kind.

A 25W charger still works with them and is a sensible buy if you'll upgrade, but the phone sets the ceiling. iPhone 12 mini and 13 mini top out at 12W.

The iPhone 16e has no MagSafe magnets, so it won't snap onto a magnetic stand or car mount, and Apple's tech specs list only Qi wireless charging. Apple's MagSafe Charger charges Qi iPhones at up to 7.5W. Anker lists the 16e as not compatible with its Prime 3-in-1.

Apple's specs list MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging at up to 25W for the iPhone Duo, and 50% in around 30 minutes with a MagSafe Charger and a 35W or higher adapter. Apple measured that with the phone open. Most third-party compatibility lists don't name the Duo yet, because it's so new.
 Do MagSafe chargers work through a case? A MagSafe case, yes. A thick or non-magnetic case, often not. Anker says its Prime 3-in-1 needs no case or a MagSafe case no thicker than 2.5 mm for 25W, Belkin lists cases up to 3 mm for its 2-in-1, and UGREEN's car mount needs a MagSafe case or none. UGREEN MagFlow Pro Qi2 25W 3-in-1 Wireless Charger review: fast, tidy and built for the Apple ecosystem

 BUY 
 TL;DR: UGREEN’s 25W Qi2 Cooling Wireless Charging Stand combines fast magnetic charging with TEC active cooling, a useful status display and a secondary 5W charging pad. It’s clever, technically interesting and particularly appealing for compatible 25W Qi2 phones, but the $79.99 price, 45W adapter requirement and lack of Apple Watch charging keep it firmly in enthusiast territory.
 UGREEN MagFlow 25W Qi2.2 3-in-1 
 4.8 
 Criteria 
 4.8 out of 5 
 BUY 
 Wireless charging has spent years selling convenience while quietly asking us to accept its biggest weakness: heat. Push more power through an inductive charger and physics inevitably turns up like an uninvited boss battle, converting some of that energy into warmth rather than useful battery percentage. With Qi2 now pushing compatible phones to 25W, thermal management matters considerably more than it did when 7.5W and 15W charging were considered quick.
 The UGREEN 25W Qi2 Cooling Wireless Charging Stand, model W776, attacks that problem with considerably more hardware than the average magnetic charging puck. It combines 25W Qi2 magnetic charging with a thermoelectric cooling system, active fan, secondary 5W charging pad and an integrated display showing charging information. It is essentially what happens when someone looks at a wireless charger and decides it needs its own cooling solution and dashboard.
 That sounds gloriously excessive. More importantly, though, there is some solid logic behind it.
 25W wireless charging makes cooling more than a party trick
 The headline feature is support for up to 25W Qi2 wireless charging on compatible devices, including supported iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 models. Older MagSafe-compatible iPhones from the iPhone 12 through iPhone 15 generation are limited to 15W, so buying a 25W charger does not magically unlock additional charging performance on hardware that cannot accept it. Qi2’s magnetic alignment is equally important because keeping the transmitter and receiver coils correctly positioned improves efficiency instead of leaving you playing wireless-charging Tetris every time you put the phone down.
 UGREEN recommends a power adapter capable of supplying at least 45W when you want maximum charging performance alongside active cooling. That requirement makes sense because the charger isn’t merely feeding the phone; it also has to power its cooling hardware, display and secondary charging surface. The wall adapter therefore becomes part of the performance equation, and anyone pairing this stand with an ancient low-wattage USB-C brick is leaving much of its capability sitting in the garage.
 The interesting part is what happens after charging begins. Higher wireless charging speeds make thermal management increasingly important because excess heat can cause charging systems to reduce power. Instead of relying purely on passive heat dissipation and software-controlled power reductions, UGREEN has put a TEC thermoelectric cooling system and fan behind the magnetic charging surface.
 That’s a much more aggressive solution than the temperature sensors commonly found inside wireless chargers. Rather than simply watching the thermometer and backing away when things become uncomfortable, the W776 is designed to actively pull heat away from the phone. UGREEN claims the cooling system can bring the phone below 20°C under its specified conditions, although that is a manufacturer claim rather than a temperature result I independently measured.
 Conceptually, however, active cooling is exactly the direction high-powered wireless charging should be exploring. Making wireless charging faster while ignoring its thermal penalty would be like overclocking a gaming PC and deciding airflow is optional.
 The little display turns invisible charging data into something useful
 Wireless chargers aren’t particularly communicative gadgets. You normally get an LED that translates roughly to “something is happening,” and that’s your lot. UGREEN’s integrated screen makes the W776 substantially more interesting because it can display the current charging power and temperature rather than hiding everything behind a mysterious blinking light.
 There is practical value here beyond satisfying the part of my brain that enjoys watching numbers change. Wireless charging performance depends on the phone, battery state, temperature and available input power, so seeing charging wattage gives you some indication of what the system is actually doing. The display can also indicate insufficient input power when the connected adapter isn’t providing the required 45W.
 Controls on the base let you switch the displayed information, while a long press adjusts screen brightness. That’s particularly useful if the stand ends up next to a bed, where even a tiny display can transform into the Eye of Sauron at 2am. UGREEN also allows the active cooling system to be disabled by double-tapping its dedicated control.
 That last option matters because active cooling introduces something ordinary charging pads don’t have: a fan. Fans create noise, however small, and not everyone will want one spinning beside their head overnight. Giving users control over cooling makes the stand considerably more flexible than permanently tying the fan to every charging session.
 A charging stand first, miniature cooling rig second
 UGREEN hasn’t allowed all that additional engineering to completely overwhelm the basic job of holding a phone. The magnetic charging surface can tilt vertically through as much as 90 degrees, while the attached phone can rotate through 360 degrees. That allows portrait and landscape positioning without disconnecting from power.
 Landscape positioning is particularly useful for Apple’s StandBy feature, turning a charging iPhone into a bedside clock, photo display or information panel. On a desk, adjustable positioning also makes notifications, video calls and media easier to see without picking up the phone every five minutes. Magnetic charging stands have always had this ergonomic advantage over flat pads, and adding active cooling doesn’t change that.
 The base contains another wireless charging surface delivering up to 5W, intended for devices such as AirPods. This makes the W776 a 2-in-1 solution rather than an Apple-everything charging shrine. Apple Watch owners will therefore still need another charging connection rather than consolidating all three devices onto this stand.
 Whether that’s a disadvantage depends on what actually lives on your desk. For someone carrying an iPhone and wireless earbuds, two charging surfaces are enough and avoid making the stand unnecessarily large. Someone deeply embedded in the Apple Watch ecosystem may reasonably prefer a 3-in-1 Qi2 station, even if that means giving up some of the W776’s more unusual cooling hardware.
 The cooling system is the reason this charger exists
 There are already plenty of Qi2 charging stands, including several from UGREEN itself. That makes active cooling the feature that needs to justify the W776’s existence, and on paper it addresses one of the most stubborn compromises associated with fast wireless power.
 Traditional wireless charging is inherently less efficient than connecting a cable directly to the phone. Some energy becomes heat, and pushing charging rates higher makes managing that heat increasingly important. Temperature can also influence how aggressively a phone is willing to accept power, which means a charger capable of delivering 25W doesn’t guarantee the phone will continuously request 25W throughout a charging session.
 The TEC cooler therefore isn’t there simply to make the specification sheet look as though it escaped from a gaming laptop. By actively moving heat away from the phone and exhausting it with a fan, the system is designed to create better thermal conditions for sustained fast charging. That is a more technically interesting approach than simply advertising a maximum wattage and ignoring what happens after the first few minutes.
 There are trade-offs. Active cooling requires additional power, adds mechanical complexity and introduces fan noise into something that would otherwise operate silently. It also helps explain the 45W input recommendation despite the phone itself receiving a maximum of 25W wirelessly. This is less elegant than a passive charging puck, but engineering often involves choosing which compromise annoys you least.
 The $79.99 price puts the W776 into enthusiast territory
 The UGREEN W776 launched at $79.99, which immediately separates it from basic Qi2 charging pads. You’re paying for more than the coil and magnets here: the additional cost buys the TEC cooling hardware, fan, display, adjustable stand mechanism and second charging surface.
 That makes the value proposition unusually dependent on how you charge. If your phone spends every night leisurely charging while you sleep, paying extra for active cooling and a wattage display is difficult to justify. A simpler Qi2 stand can accomplish the fundamental task with fewer components and less money.
 The argument becomes stronger for people who regularly need substantial battery recovery during shorter charging windows. That’s where faster Qi2 charging and thermal management make more sense together. Someone topping up a phone between meetings, gaming sessions or trips is more likely to appreciate hardware designed around maintaining better charging conditions than someone whose handset has eight uninterrupted hours to reach 100%.
 There is also an undeniable enthusiast appeal. Watching real-time charging information while a thermoelectric cooler works behind your iPhone is magnificently nerdy for a product whose ancestors were essentially plastic circles with cables attached. Not everyone needs that, but then nobody  needed  RGB RAM either, and look how that turned out.
 Compatibility matters before you spend the money
 The biggest reason not to buy the UGREEN 25W Qi2 Cooling Wireless Charging Stand is simple: your phone may not benefit from its headline charging speed. Compatible newer devices can take advantage of the 25W Qi2 capability, while older MagSafe iPhones remain limited to 15W. The charger is backward compatible, but backward compatibility isn’t the same thing as a free performance upgrade.
 You’ll also need suitable magnetic alignment or an appropriate compatible case where required. Qi2’s magnetic system is one of its biggest advantages because proper coil positioning reduces the uncertainty traditionally associated with wireless charging, but cases can still affect the experience when they aren’t designed for magnetic charging.
 Then there is the power adapter. The stand requires at least a 45W-capable supply for its maximum charging-and-cooling configuration, making the adapter specification something worth checking before blaming the charger for disappointing performance. High-speed wireless charging has reached the point where the entire power chain matters.
 This isn’t unique to UGREEN. As wireless charging becomes more powerful, the days of plugging an advanced charger into whatever forgotten USB brick happens to be lurking behind the sofa are increasingly over.
 Verdict
 The UGREEN 25W Qi2 Cooling Wireless Charging Stand takes a genuinely interesting approach to the thermal problem created by faster wireless charging. Combining 25W Qi2 support with TEC cooling and an active fan gives the hardware a technical purpose beyond simply adding another number to the box, while the real-time power and temperature display provides useful visibility into what is normally an invisible process.
 Its adjustable magnetic mount, 360-degree phone rotation and secondary 5W pad make it practical as a desktop or bedside charger, although the lack of integrated Apple Watch charging means it isn’t the complete Apple-device docking station some buyers will want. The requirement for a 45W power adapter also needs to be factored into the setup, and active cooling inevitably makes this more complicated than a silent passive stand.
 At $79.99, this is enthusiast charging hardware rather than an essential upgrade for everyone. Owners of compatible 25W Qi2 devices who frequently rely on quick wireless top-ups have the strongest reason to consider it, particularly if heat has been a frustration with previous chargers. Owners of older 15W devices, overnight-only chargers and anyone simply looking for the cheapest route to magnetic wireless power can comfortably spend less.
 UGREEN hasn’t reinvented wireless charging here. It has simply confronted one of its oldest enemies with a fan, a thermoelectric cooler and a tiny screen, which is an appropriately geeky solution to a very real problem.

 is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years. 
 Despite my initial skepticism, I’m now sold on wireless Qi chargers that add integrated fans to keep your phone cool while charging. I figured they’d be too loud, or too weak, or too gimmicky, but I’m a convert after spending a week with the new $59.99 Kuxiu D5 Qi2.2 charging dock. Its active cooling system has kept my phone from heating up, unlike every other Qi charger I’ve tried. Good thing, given my own history with an overheating phone.
 Last year I fried the logic board on my titanium iPhone 15 Pro. I was on a sweltering train and trying to edit a 4K video on my phone, which was charging from a magnetically attached Qi power bank . Oof, my iPhone is getting really hot , I thought, just as the screen went forever blank. The repair bill was €660.33 (over $750), for which I paid nothing because it was just inside the two-year warranty. Apple’s “genius” wouldn’t say if the phone overheated, but I’m not keen to tempt fate twice.
 Heat is the enemy of batteries
 Heat is the enemy of batteries. High temperatures accelerate the chemical degradation of lithium-ion cells, permanently reducing how much charge they can hold over time. The electromagnetic induction employed by Qi chargers is inherently inefficient, producing far more heat than transferring electricity through a cable plugged into your phone. That heat can cause phones to throttle the wireless charging speed in order to protect the battery.
 Despite knowing this, I keep coming back to Qi charging docks and power banks because they’re so damn convenient. I’m also addicted to Apple’s StandBy feature that turns my phone into a desk or bedside clock and widget machine when docked and charging in landscape orientation.
 Fortunately, companies like Anker, Aukey, ESR, and Kuxiu have started building active cooling systems directly into their Qi chargers. They feature tiny heat sinks and ultra-quiet internal fans that actively blow the heat away from the back of your phone while it charges. This keeps the battery significantly cooler and allows for faster charging speeds. Powerful magnets ensure perfect alignment between the phone’s receiver coil and the charger’s transmitter coil to maximize efficiency and minimize heat waste.
 The display on the D5 shows the charging status of up to three devices, and whether the active cooling is enabled. 
 A look from behind at the cooling fan beneath the Qi2.2 phone charger. 
 This button lets you switch off the display, switch off active cooling, and retract the watch charger. 
 The 45W GAN charger is a great in-the-box addition for such an inexpensive Qi2.2 charging dock. Here the watch charger is shown recessed. 
 The fan inside the Kuxiu D5 operates silently, but it can still be turned off if you want. The display is useful, but the little winky-faced screensaver is not. I do like knowing the time and how much charge each device is pulling, in addition to the total power draw, but the animated movement is distracting when caught out of the corner of my eye. It’s also a bit too bright for my taste when perched on my nightstand. Fortunately, I can turn the display off with a tap of a button.
 I like that the Kuxiu D5 ships with a 45W USB-C PD charger in the box. Otherwise, you’d have to guess if whatever charger you have lying around will support the dock’s max total output, which can deliver up to 25W to Qi2.2-compatible phones, 2.5W to Qi-compatible watches, and 5W to Qi-compatible earbuds. It’s compatible with several generations of phones, watches, and earbuds sold by Apple, Samsung, and others.
 Kuxiu calls the D5 a “5-in-1” charger, which I find misleading since it’ll only charge up to three devices simultaneously. It seems to include the display and fan in its total. By that count, I’d be happier if this was a 4-in-1 device, since the added cost for the display won’t add much value for most people, and it can only cause issues down the road.
 The watch charger is also a little silly in its over-engineering. A long-press on the dock’s sole button kicks off a tiny motor to slowly push the watch dock out the side. I guess it adds to the blocky dock’s durability when traveling, but not by much, and it can only be retracted when the dock is plugged into the wall.
 1 / 9 Works great with Apple’s StandBy mode for photo slideshows while the D5 keeps your iPhone cool. 
 Overall the Kuxiu D5 is a fine Qi2.2 charging dock made better by active cooling. It’s equally at home on a desktop or nightstand, and priced below similar docks from Anker , ESR , and others .
 Active cooling on Qi chargers is a good idea whose time has come. Phones sold by Huawei, Xiaomi, and Oppo have supported wireless charging speeds of 50W and above for years . But that’s only possible when placed on proprietary charging docks capable of whisking away all the extra waste heat. Now the body responsible for Qi is working on a global 50W standard for release by 2028 . Manufacturers will likely need to adopt active cooling to reliably sustain those higher charging rates.
 Fine by me. Whatever it takes to keep that vital Qi life force flowing.

It cools less aggressively than a TEC plate in theory, but it uses less power and is a simpler failure mode: fans are mechanical and can become noisy over time, whereas a solid-state plate has no moving parts but depends on a strong supply.
 When you evaluate a fan-cooled mount, read the noise comments in reviews you trust, and consider your car. In a quiet electric vehicle, a small whirr is audible; in a diesel pickup, it will never be noticed. If you are a light sleeper on long highway drives, noise is a real selection criterion and not a footnote.
 Pros: 
 Fan cooling in a mid-range tier
 Brand offers a full ladder from 15W to 25W
 Simple magnetic attachment
 Cons: 
 Mount details differ between models, so confirm the exact version
 Fan may be audible in a very quiet cabin
 5. Beeasy 25W Qi2.2 with Vacuum Suction Cup: Best for Windshield or Dash
 25W Qi2.2 magnetic wireless charging
 Built-in cooling fan
 Upgraded vacuum suction cup per the listing
 360-degree rotation
 Mid-range tier
 Best for: drivers with trucks, vans or SUVs where the dashboard sits far away from the driver and a vent mount feels too low. Skip if: your windshield is heavily tinted at the mounting point or local regulations restrict windshield mounts.
 Beeasy approaches the problem with a vacuum suction cup rather than a vent clip, which changes how you place the phone. A suction cup lets you choose almost any glass or smooth plastic area, from the lower windshield to the center of the dash. The upside is height and reach; the downside is that the phone now faces direct sun more often, which is the exact situation where active cooling earns its keep. Because the phone is in sunlight, the cooling fan may run longer, which draws more power and may be audible.
 Before you commit, think about what you are sticking the suction cup to. Glass is easy. Textured, leather-grain or coated dashboards usually are not. If you must use a dash, clean it with a lint-free cloth and a little isopropyl alcohol, let it dry, and press the cup firmly. If it loses grip in summer heat, move it to the glass. This is general suction-mount advice; always follow the maker’s installation steps.
 Pros: 
 Flexible mounting position
 Cooling fan plus 25W Qi2.2
 360-degree rotation for angle control
 Cons: 
 Suction cups need a clean flat surface
 Sun exposure keeps the cooling system busy
 6. TOUGH ON Qi2.2 25W with Cooling Fan: Best When You Want a Power Supply Bundled
 Qi2.2 25W magnetic wireless charging
 Cooling fan
 Listing mentions a 45W adapter alongside the mount; confirm what is included before buying
 Air vent magnetic mount
 Mid-range tier
 Best for: buyers who do not own a 45W USB-C car charger and would rather buy one box than two. Skip if: you already own a high-wattage car charger and would pay for a duplicate.
 The reason this model is on the list is the adapter. The 45W figure appears in the listing text, and the earlier models explicitly demand a 45W-class supply for full cooling, which makes a bundled adapter a convenient detail. The caution is simple: listing titles on marketplaces sometimes mention accessories that are sold as options, so read the in-the-box section before you assume everything is included. If the adapter is not in the box, price the mount plus a separate adapter and compare that total to the UGREEN and Spigen setups.
 The vent mount design places this closer to the UGREEN than to the suction models. The same rules apply: check your vent slat width and shape, and plan how you will route the cable so it does not tug the phone away from the magnet on a pothole.
 Pros: 
 Adapter mentioned in the listing
 25W Qi2.2 with a cooling fan
 Vent mount keeps the dash clear
 Cons: 
 Box contents need confirming
 Less brand history than ESR or Spigen
 Also Consider
 ESR 15W CryoBoost Magnetic Car Mount
 The older ESR design charges at 15W and includes the CryoBoost cooling plate, according to the listing. If you do not need 25W or your iPhone only supports 15W magnetic charging, this is a lower tier way to keep the cooling feature. It sits in the budget-to-mid range.
 INIU 3-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Car Charger
 The INIU listing mentions a cooling fan, an extra clamp for bumpy roads and Qi2 certification. The extra clamp is a useful idea for drivers on rough roads, where the magnet alone might not hold a heavy phone with a thick case. Budget tier.
 Angkel Qi2 25W with Ice Cooling
 Angkel is the lowest-tier option in this group and lists Qi2 25W, RGB light and ice cooling. Budget mounts can be fine, but check the certification details and read the fine print on what adapter is required. Skip it if you want documented compatibility.
 Esoulk Qi2 25W Cup Holder Mount with TEC Cooling
 If your car has no good vent or windshield position, a cup-holder mount with a long arm may be the answer. The Esoulk listing mentions TEC cooling and Qi2.2 25W. Check the arm length against your cup holder position, and note it is in the premium tier.
 How We Chose
 We started with the question a driver would actually ask: which Qi2 magnetic car chargers claim active cooling, and which of them are real products with stated specifications? We pulled candidates from the product store catalog, kept only models that explicitly name a cooling system (fan, TEC, Peltier or CryoBoost), and then compared them on charging standard, mount type, cooling mechanism, power-adapter requirements and price tier. We cross-checked one model, the UGREEN mount, against the maker’s product information and independent coverage of the Qi2.2 standard. We limited the main list to two products per brand at most.
 To be plain about it, we did not personally use these products. This guide is research-based and draws on manufacturer specification sheets, marketplace listing details and independent reviews and product coverage, and we say “not listed” where a detail was not confirmed. Where a listing’s own wording implies something that we could not confirm (for example, an adapter included in the box), we say so instead of presenting it as fact. Specific prices are intentionally omitted because they change often; we use price tiers instead.
 Buying Guide
 Check your iPhone and the real wattage
 Only some iPhones can use the full 25W Qi2.2 speed. Per UGREEN’s information, 25W applies to recent iPhone 16 and 17 series models on a current iOS release. Older magnetic iPhones, such as the 12 through 15 series, can still charge on a Qi2 or MagSafe-style mount but at lower speeds. If your phone is in that group, a 15W mount will give essentially the same experience for less money, and an active-cooled 15W model like the ESR 15W is a sensible choice.
 Match the power adapter to the cooling
 Treat 45W as the working minimum for a 25W mount with active cooling, as the UGREEN and Spigen information indicates. A 20W phone charger leaves little headroom. Look for a single-port or high-wattage USB-C PD output on your 12V car charger and make sure the cable is the one that came with the mount or a cable rated for the same power. A weak cable is a common reason people say their fast charger is not fast.
 Choose a mount style for your car
 Vent clips work well in most cars with horizontal or vertical louvers, but they do not fit round vents and can sag if the vent slats are thin. Suction cups work on glass and smooth dashboards but not on grained or soft-touch surfaces. Cup-holder mounts suit cars with centre consoles and long arms, but they place the phone low. Always check local rules about windshield mounts: some regions restrict mounting anything in the driver’s line of sight.
 Decide between a fan and a thermoelectric plate
 A fan is simple and low power but may make noise. A TEC or Peltier plate cools the charging surface directly and often pairs with a fan, which means more cooling at the cost of higher power draw. If you charge on long summer drives with navigation running, choose a TEC design. If you take short city trips, the difference is minor.
 Think about your phone case
 Magnetic car chargers work best with a case that supports MagSafe-style attachment. Thick cases, wallet cases and metal plates between phone and case can weaken the magnet and block efficient charging. If your case is not magnetic, remove the phone from the case or choose a case designed for Qi2.
 Common Mistakes to Avoid
 Plugging a 25W mount into a low-power adapter, then blaming the mount for slow charging.
 Mounting a suction cup on a textured dashboard and expecting it to hold in summer heat.
 Leaving the phone on the mount in a parked car in direct sun. Active cooling needs power and does not make a hot parked car safe for a phone.
 Ignoring the case. A thick non-magnetic case is one of the most common reasons magnetic car mounts disappoint.
 Assuming every Qi2 mount is actually Qi2.2 25W. Read the wattage and standard in the listing carefully.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is active cooling worth it in a car phone charger?
 Active cooling is worth it if you use navigation and charge at the same time in warm weather, because phones slow charging when hot. In mild weather or on short drives, a non-cooled mount is usually enough.
 Do I need a 45W adapter for a 25W Qi2.2 car charger?
 For mounts with active cooling, yes in most cases. The UGREEN information says a 45W or higher PD adapter is needed for full cooling performance, and the Spigen listing says a 45W adapter is required. Follow the maker’s note for your model.
 Which iPhones get 25W on a Qi2.2 mount?
 According to the UGREEN information we reviewed, 25W applies to iPhone 16 and 17 series models running a current iOS release. Older iPhones charge more slowly. Check your phone against the maker’s compatibility list.
 Will a magnetic car charger hold my phone on a bumpy road?
 It can, if your case supports magnetic attachment and the magnet ring is strong. On rough roads, consider mounts with an extra clamp or a stronger magnet, and avoid heavy cases that weaken the magnet.
 Are fan-cooled mounts noisy?
 Some are. Fans move air and may be audible in a quiet cabin. Thermoelectric plates are quieter by themselves but usually include a fan too. Look for the noise comments in reviews you trust.
 Can I use a Qi2 car charger with an Android phone?
 Some Android phones support Qi2 magnetic charging, but many need a magnetic case to attach. Non-iPhone devices may charge slower on these mounts. Verify compatibility with the maker.
 Is it safe to leave my phone on the charger in direct sun?
 Phones can overheat in direct sun regardless of charging, and active cooling does not remove that risk. Avoid leaving a phone on the mount in a parked, hot car, and follow the guidance from your phone’s maker on operating temperatures.
 Which One Should You Buy?
 If you have a recent iPhone and a standard vent, buy the UGREEN Qi2.2 25W mount, add a 45W-class USB-C car charger, and you have the best-documented cooling setup in this group. If you want a premium build and a familiar accessory brand, choose the ESR OmniLock. If you prefer a suction mount, the Spigen is the value pick and the Beeasy is the flexible-position pick. Pick TOUGH ON when a bundled adapter saves you a separate purchase and you have confirmed the box contents. If your iPhone is older, a 15W model with cooling such as the ESR 15W or the INIU is more sensible than paying for 25W you will not use.

I tested Qi2 wireless chargers with cooling solutions - here's how my buying advice changed 
 Skip to main content

 ZDNET's key takeaways
 Magnetic wireless chargers use different methods to fight heat.
 I tested three different stations to see which works best.
 The results were surprising.
 To those of us who have been longtime fans of wireless charging -- even going back to the days of the Palm Pre -- one thing has remained certain: When you pick up your phone , it's going to be warm. 
 As it turns out, transmitting electricity through the air is going to heat things up, and that can be not ideal for your battery. When I got on the phone with the folks at Mophie, they were excited to tell me about its new charging stand.
 Also: I cracked open a '1,000W' portable charger after it failed me in minutes - and wished I hadn't 
 According to CMO Brian Oleska, the 4-in-1 charger features StealthCharge Technology , which is Qi2.2-certified for 25W of wireless charging. But it passively keeps your phone cooler by positioning most of the charging components away from the charging pad and in the base of the stand. The metal of the stand acts as a heat sink, keeping your phone cooler.  
 Advertisement
 Advertisement
 As for the charging coil, it comes with its own heat sink. In theory, this keeps your phone and its battery cooler overall, and it's also silent -- there's no fan cooling the charger.
 Testing with Apple and Google
 So, I wanted to test it out. 
 Mophie sent the 4-in-1 charging stand, which includes a watch charger, an additional Qi pad for AirPods, and a retractable wired cable as well. I tested this charger against a Ugreen Qi2 25W Magflow wireless charger, which monitors the temperature of the phone to prevent overheating, and an ESR Qi2.2 3-in-1 charging station with its CryoBoost fan-cooling technology.
 To conduct the test, I used an iPhone Air and a Google Pixel 10, both of which have integrated magnets in the back of the phone to support Qi2.2 charging. The iPhone Air supports up to 20W of wireless charging, and the Pixel 10 supports up to 15W. Of course, we've learned that the wattage advertised by phone companies isn't necessarily what you're getting .
 Adam Doud / ZDNET
 For testing, I discharged the phone to somewhere below 20%, and I charged the phone for 30 minutes using each stand. 
 Advertisement
 Advertisement
 Then, I measured the heat of the charging pad on the charger itself, the back of the phone (on the logo), and the camera bump with a thermometer gun. I measured the camera island on each phone for different reasons. 
 The iPhone Air famously keeps its processor (and basically everything else) in the camera pill, while the visor on the back of the Pixel 10 is the only metal component on the back of the phone, so if there's a good place to find heat, it's there.
 Here's what happened
 Of the three chargers, the ESR kept both phones cooler, with temperature increases of 13.1 and 14.8 degrees Fahrenheit for the iPhone Air and the Pixel 10, respectively. That's not surprising, since it uses an active cooling mechanism (read: a fan). According to Mophie, the benefit of using its charger is that it's silent since there is no fan. 
 Practically speaking, the fan in the ESR charger is basically a non-issue. Yes, there is noise, but it's incredibly faint.
 Adam Doud / ZDNET
 The Mophie charger kept the charging pad and the iPhone Air cooler, but the Pixel 10 and charging pad were cooler on the Ugreen charger than on the Mophie charger. The Ugreen charger doesn't have a cooling mechanism except for an internal heat monitor that can adjust charging levels on the fly. Then again, that's with an Android phone, and the Mophie charger is designed for the iPhone. 
 Advertisement
 Advertisement
 From an engineering standpoint, I'm not 100% positive what difference that makes.
 Also: I cracked open cheap charging gadgets from Temu - and it was worse than I expected 
 Finally, just for fun, I plugged in the iPhone Air to a wired charger for 30 minutes. 
 It charged 44% of the battery, and it increased the temperature of the battery by 17.1 degrees -- about the same as the Ugreen wireless charger -- and it increased the camera island temperature by 23.9 degrees. So, overall, wired charging heated up the iPhone more than any of the wireless chargers, which makes sense, but I never really thought about it before.
 Advertisement
 Advertisement
 Overall, it makes me wonder if heat is really the problem. Now, I'm not so sure. 
 But what I have learned is that the method by which your wireless charging stand tries to dissipate heat isn't as important as other things, such as whether it can charge other devices and how portable it is overall. At the end of the day, a charging phone is going to get warm, and there's not a heck of a lot you can do about it.
